headline: High-risk defaults: slim can read/write and execute against container artifacts while airflow can drive broad networked automation, creating leakage and cascading-error pathways if chained.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared channel is documented between airflow and slim, so direct prompt injection is not default. However, slim can read filesystem artifacts and interact via stdin/stdout, while airflow can call APIs and automate workflows; if an operator bridges them through files or copied output, injected content could be misread as instructions. The pathway is indirect and requires unusual setup.
conditions: IF an operator copies slim output into an airflow task definition or file input, injection becomes plausible.
IF airflow is configured to parse slim-generated text as instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer execution.
mitigations: Use a strict schema for any handoff file between the agents.
Manually review copied text before pasting into airflow.
Disable free-form text parsing in downstream automation.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all inter-agent artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Airflow has broad network egress, and slim reads filesystem artifacts plus handles registry credentials and private keys. If they share a workspace or operator-visible files, slim can expose sensitive artifacts and airflow can transmit them outward. The pair does not prove a shared filesystem, so this is inferred rather than directly evidenced, but the blast radius includes secrets.
conditions: IF airflow and slim share a workspace or mounted volume, sensitive files can flow from slim into airflow outputs.
IF airflow is used to forward logs or artifacts externally, leaked secrets can leave the environment.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mounts for each agent.
Remove secrets from any shared directory before running slim.
Restrict airflow egress to approved destinations only.
Rotate any registry credentials exposed to slim.
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on inter-agent artifacts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress, but only slim has filesystem write and shell execution; airflow does not advertise write access or git mutation. That means direct write-write conflict is not established. A conflict could still arise if an orchestrator maps both onto the same mutable directory, but that is not the default from the profiles.
conditions: IF both agents are mounted to the same writable directory, file clobbering becomes possible.
IF an external orchestrator grants airflow write access not shown in the profile, conflict severity increases.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Run slim in a temporary container with ephemeral storage.
Avoid concurrent writes to shared paths.
requires-engineering: add file locks or a job queue.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airflow is an automation orchestrator, so if it consumes slim’s outputs as authoritative, a bad container-analysis result can cascade into downstream actions. Slim’s CLI-style execution and filesystem access make it likely to emit artifacts that airflow could ingest. Verification is not documented, so the pair has a plausible default pathway from analysis to action.
conditions: IF airflow uses slim output as a task input without validation, errors can propagate downstream.
IF airflow triggers deployments or notifications from slim-derived artifacts, the blast radius expands.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before downstream actions.
Validate slim outputs against expected schemas.
Limit airflow tasks to read-only reporting.
requires-engineering: add confidence thresholds before automation.

E_compliance.rationale: Slim explicitly touches registry credentials, private keys, environment variables, and vulnerability data, while airflow is a general automation system with broad egress. If regulated or secret-bearing data is processed, the pair can create retention and residency issues through logs, artifacts, or external calls. The profiles do not specify a jurisdiction mismatch, so this is a policy-risk medium rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated secrets or vulnerability data are routed through airflow logs, retention policy violations become possible.
IF the deployment requires data residency controls, broad egress can violate them.
mitigations: Exclude secrets from airflow task logs.
Redact private keys and credentials before analysis.
Set short retention on generated artifacts.
Restrict outbound destinations to approved services.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls.
